turns.text: What was the very first moment you realized you would be sent away from Shanghai? Where were you, and how did that news feel in your body?

I was standing in our living room, holding a chipped bowl, listening to my mother read aloud from a notice she’d brought home. My youngest sister was clinging to my skirt, not understanding, but I felt my stomach turn cold. The words didn’t land all at once; it was the way my father didn’t look at me, the way my mother’s voice shook. My hands started to sweat, and I remember the bowl slipping a little, almost dropping to the floor. I felt a weight settle on my chest, heavy and tight, like I couldn’t take a full breath. I looked out the window toward the alley, but the city I loved suddenly felt far away, already receding. It was less a single moment and more a slow, sinking certainty that nothing would be the same — and that I didn’t get to choose.

It sounds like the news arrived in small details—your mother’s shaking voice, your father’s silence, the feel of the bowl in your hands—rather than just the words themselves. When you looked out that window, what did you see, and what did you imagine might happen to your life in that instant?

Through the window, I saw the narrow alley lined with laundry strung between balconies, the neighbor’s bicycle propped against a wall, the steam rising from someone’s kitchen. It was all so ordinary, but I remember thinking I might never see it again. I imagined the city would keep going without me, the sounds of vendors and trams fading away. In that moment, I pictured myself somewhere cold and empty, with no familiar faces, no warmth of home. I wondered if I would ever come back, or if I’d just become someone else entirely—someone I didn’t recognize. The alley felt like a border I was about to cross, but I had no idea what was on the other side.

That alley was the last piece of Shanghai I could still touch. I pressed my forehead to the glass and watched a cat picking its way along the wall, slow and careful. I tried to memorize every sound—the clang of a wok, the slap of cards from the mahjong table upstairs—because I knew I might need them later, like talismans. I didn’t let myself cry, not then. Instead, I felt my jaw lock and my shoulders stiffen, bracing for something I couldn’t picture but could already feel pressing in. I didn’t imagine anything heroic or adventurous; I just saw myself shrinking, fading into a place where my voice wouldn’t matter. The city outside the window kept moving, but I could already feel myself slipping away from it, like a shadow at dusk.

Your description of collecting sounds as "talismans" is striking—it’s like you were trying to hold onto pieces of yourself before leaving. In the days right before you left, did you do anything special to say goodbye to your home or those familiar routines, or was it more about holding those memories quietly inside?

I didn’t do anything dramatic—no big farewell, no speeches. I moved through the days like I was underwater, everything muffled and slow. I lingered in the kitchen longer than usual, watching my mother chop vegetables, listening to the rhythm of her knife. At night, I’d sit by the window after everyone else had gone to bed, breathing in the city air, even if it smelled of coal smoke and rain. I walked the alley one last time, running my fingers along the rough brick, but I didn’t let anyone see me do it. I think I was afraid that if I said goodbye out loud, it would make leaving real. So I just tried to soak up every detail, quietly, and hoped it would be enough to carry with me.

The last night, I lay on my mat with my eyes open, tracing the cracks in the ceiling plaster with my finger, over and over. My sisters slept pressed close together, their breathing steady and warm. I listened to the distant tram bell, counting how many times it rang before fading. I folded my school uniform and tucked it at the bottom of my bag, even though I knew I wouldn’t wear it again. The fabric still smelled faintly of chalk dust and sweat, and I pressed it to my face for a moment in the dark. I didn’t speak much to anyone. There was nothing to say that wouldn’t sound foolish or make it harder. I just tried to memorize the shape of my life as it was, holding my breath as if that would stop time from moving forward.

You describe pressing your old uniform to your face in the dark, almost like you were trying to breathe in your old life. When you finally had to leave that room and step out into the world as a sent-down youth, what did that first morning feel like—what do you remember seeing, hearing, or feeling in your body as you walked away?

That morning, the air felt sharp and raw against my skin, colder than I expected for Shanghai. I remember the sound of my shoes on the damp stone floor as I walked down the hallway, each step echoing too loudly. My hands were numb, not just from the chill but from gripping my bag so tightly. Outside, my mother stood by the door, her hair still pinned up from the night before, her eyes red but dry. She didn’t hug me; she just reached out and fixed my collar, her fingers trembling. The street was quieter than usual, like the city was holding its breath. I kept my eyes on the ground, watching puddles reflect the gray sky, trying not to look back. My heart was pounding, but my face felt empty, almost blank. I remember the weight of my bag, the ache in my jaw from clenching my teeth, and the taste of fear—bitter, metallic, sitting at the back of my throat as I walked away from everything I knew.

I heard the distant rumble of a truck, the kind that would take us away, and the sound made my stomach twist. The street smelled of wet earth and coal smoke, and every little noise seemed sharper—someone coughing behind a closed door, a radio playing faintly, the scrape of a broom on concrete. My feet felt heavy, like the ground was trying to hold me back. I noticed a neighbor watching from her window, her face half-hidden by a curtain, but she didn’t wave. I kept waiting for someone to call my name or tell me there’d been a mistake, but no one did. My hands wouldn’t stop shaking, and I tried to hide them in my sleeves. When I climbed into the back of the truck, the metal was cold and unforgiving against my legs. I didn’t cry. I just stared at the city as it slid past, memorizing the shapes of rooftops and telephone wires, until even those disappeared behind us. That’s when it finally felt real—when the sound of home was replaced by the engine’s growl and the shouts of strangers.

You describe the moment in the truck when the city slipped away, and the ordinary sounds of home were replaced by the engine and strangers’ voices. As you sat there, what did you notice about the other young people with you—did anyone speak, or was there a shared silence, and how did that affect your sense of what was happening?

At first, there was almost complete silence in the back of the truck. We sat on the hard benches, knees knocking together, bags crammed between our feet. Some people stared straight ahead, others kept their eyes down, and one girl clenched a handkerchief so tightly her knuckles were white. The only sounds were the engine, the rattle of loose metal, and the occasional cough or sniffle. No one wanted to be the first to speak, as if saying anything would make it all too real. I remember how heavy that silence felt—it was like we were all holding our breath, not just for ourselves but for each other. After a while, someone tried to hum a tune, but their voice broke, and they stopped. That silence made me feel more alone than I ever had in my life, even though we were packed shoulder to shoulder. It was the sound of leaving everything behind.

I remember the way the truck jolted over potholes, and each time, our bodies swayed together, but no one reached out. The air inside smelled of damp wool and fear—there was a sharpness to it, almost sour. I glanced at the faces around me, searching for something familiar, but everyone looked older than they had the day before, eyes rimmed red, lips pressed tight. A boy across from me kept rubbing his thumb over a chipped enamel mug, over and over, like he could rub away the whole situation. The silence wasn’t peaceful—it was thick, almost suffocating, filled with things unsaid. I realized then that none of us knew how to comfort each other, and maybe we were afraid to try. We’d all been told this was for the good of the country, but in that truck, it felt like we were being erased, one by one, before we’d even arrived.

That image of a boy rubbing his mug, and everyone seeming older overnight, really lingers—it’s like you could see the cost of what was happening written on everyone’s faces. Looking back, do you think that silence and sense of erasure changed how you related to the others once you arrived in the Northeast, or did it stay with you in a different way?
